Our releases happen in two steps: upload, then switch.

**1. Upload every new asset under a versioned name.** Each file gets a name tied to its version or content hash, such as `app.3f9c2a.js` instead of `app.js`. New files never overwrite existing ones, so publishing them changes nothing for current users. Nothing references them yet.

**2. Switch the manifest to the new names.** The manifest tells the site which asset files to load. Updating it is the moment the release goes live.

**Why the upload comes first.** As soon as the manifest changes, browsers that fetch it will request the files it names. If any of those files aren't uploaded yet, or are still propagating to the CDN, users get 404s and a broken page. Uploading everything first guarantees that every file the new manifest references already exists when the first browser asks for it. This makes the switch a single, clean cutover rather than a window where the site is half-deployed.

**Why we keep the old assets.** The switch doesn't reach every browser at the same instant. A user with the site already open is running code from the previous manifest, and that code may still request old files, for example a lazy-loaded chunk when they navigate to a new section. Browsers and CDN edges may also keep serving the cached previous manifest until it expires. If we deleted the old assets at release time, all of those users would hit missing files mid-session. Keeping them lets old and new versions run side by side until the old sessions and caches age out.

Keeping old assets also makes rollback cheap: switching the manifest back to the previous names restores the prior release instantly, with no re-upload.

Every release puts files at new URLs first, then changes the one file that tells browsers which URLs to use. Nothing a browser might be using gets modified or removed during the release.

**How it works**

1. **Upload new assets under versioned names.** Each build's JS, CSS, images and fonts get names that include a version or content hash, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`. A new release never overwrites an existing file. It only adds files.
2. **Switch the manifest.** The manifest maps logical names to the current versioned files. Updating it to the new names is what actually releases the new version. Any browser that fetches the manifest after this point loads the new assets.
3. **Leave the old assets in place.** The previous release's files stay where they are.

**Why the upload comes before the switch**

The manifest can only safely reference files that already exist. If we switched it first, a browser could read the new manifest and request a file that hasn't been uploaded yet. That request would fail and the page would load broken, with missing scripts or unstyled content, until the upload finished. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when the manifest goes live. It also makes the switch a single, small, near-instant change rather than a gradual one.

**Why we keep the old assets**

A browser that loaded the page before the switch is still running against the old manifest. It may not have requested every file yet. Lazy-loaded chunks, route-specific bundles, images further down the page and fonts are often fetched minutes or hours later. Those requests still use the old versioned names. If we deleted the old files at release time, those users would hit 404s in the middle of a session even though they did nothing wrong. Keeping the old assets lets every session finish on the version it started with. The next full page load picks up the new manifest.

The same property makes rollback cheap. Pointing the manifest back at the previous names restores the old release instantly because those files are still there.

Versioned names also allow those files to be cached aggressively. A given URL's content never changes, so browsers and CDNs can keep it indefinitely without serving stale code. The manifest is the only file that has to stay fresh.

Our static-site releases happen in two steps. First, we upload every new asset (scripts, stylesheets, images) under a versioned name, so a new build never overwrites a file from an earlier one. Then we switch the manifest to point at those new names. The manifest is the file browsers read to find out which assets make up the current version of the site.

**Why the upload comes before the switch.** Once the manifest changes, browsers start requesting the new asset names right away. If any of those files weren't uploaded yet, those requests would fail and users would get a broken or half-styled page. Uploading everything first means every name in the new manifest already exists when the switch happens. The switch is then a single change from one complete version to another complete version, with no window where the site points at missing files.

**Why we keep the old assets.** A browser that loaded the site before the switch still has the previous manifest. It will keep requesting the old asset names, for example when it loads a script lazily or navigates to another page. If we deleted the old files at release time, those requests would fail for anyone in the middle of a session. Keeping the old assets lets those browsers finish working with the version they started on, while new visitors get the new version.

Our release happens in two steps: upload the new assets, then switch the manifest. Each new asset gets a versioned filename, usually a content hash such as `app.3f9a1c.js`. The manifest is the small entry file that tells the browser which asset names to load. It is typically `index.html` or a JSON map.

**Why the upload happens before the switch**

The manifest is the only thing that tells browsers which assets to request. If we switched it first, browsers would immediately request files that aren't on the server yet and get 404s, which means broken pages and missing scripts or styles. When every new asset is already in place, switching the manifest is a single atomic change. Before the switch, everyone gets the old version. After it, everyone gets the new version, and every file it references already exists. No visitor ever sees a half-released site.

**Why we keep the old assets**

When someone loads a page, their browser fetches the manifest once and may load the assets it lists much later. Lazy-loaded chunks, route-split bundles and fonts are examples. A tab opened before the release keeps the old manifest and keeps requesting old asset names. If we deleted those files during the release, those users would hit 404s partway through their session. Navigation would fail, or the app would break until they reloaded.

Because each version has unique filenames, old and new assets live side by side without conflict. That has two more benefits:

- **Caching:** an asset's name changes whenever its content changes. We can therefore cache assets forever. Only the manifest needs a short cache lifetime.
- **Rollback:** switching the manifest back to the previous names is an instant rollback. Nothing needs to be re-uploaded.

Old assets can be removed later, once no realistic session could still reference them. Usually that means a few releases or a fixed time window afterwards.
